title: Latency Can Kill: Precision and Deadline in Online Games (Claypool & Claypool, MMSys 2010)
label: research
claim: Classifies player actions by precision and deadline; latency effect depends on the action, not the genre alone. Experiment used BZFlag with 8 BOTS (not human players) at induced latencies 0/100/500/1000 ms, varying tank size (precision) and tank speed/bullet speed (deadline); smaller targets suffered more from latency. Paper cites the 'common conception' that <100 ms is needed for unimpaired play and ~100 ms as tolerable for some FPS (citing others, not measured here), 500 ms as measurable degradation for third-person avatar games. Bot-based, so it models score impact of lag, not human perception. Read via pdftotext of the full PDF, skimmed intro/method/results.

title: Latency and Player Actions in Online Games (Claypool & Claypool, CACM 2006)
label: snippet
claim: Search-summary only: latency effect depends on action precision and deadline; sniper shot on a moving target hurt most, selecting a set of items much less. Thresholds not seen.

title: Designing for low-latency direct-touch input (Ng et al, UIST 2012)
label: snippet
claim: Citation confirmed. Secondhand via a later paper: people noticed drag latency above ~5-10 ms. Patent family from same lab says effects vanish near 1 ms; patents are not the paper. Full text not retrieved (403).

title: Instantaneous human-computer interactions: button causes and screen effects (Raaen & Eg, HCII 2015)
label: snippet
claim: Button click flips a spinning disc direction after variable delay; participants judged immediate vs delayed; authors conclude humans perceive very short delays. Simula news item on Raaen PhD: average person notices ~0.2 s, some down to ~0.05 s. Exact numbers not seen in full text.

title: Sakurai Famitsu column on hitstop (fan translation, Source Gaming)
label: developer
claim: Sakurai (Smash Bros.): on a hit both parties freeze for the same time, 'emphasizing the power of impact'; stronger attacks freeze longer up to a hard cap; projectiles less; attacker and defender vibrate (hurtboxes stay put so hit consistency is kept); shake direction chosen so feet do not clip the stage; shake tapers over the freeze and scales with camera distance; hitstop kept shorter than he would like because in free-for-alls a third player can act during a freeze. No frame counts given. Fan translation, wording may differ from original.

title: Sakurai YouTube video on hit stop techniques (GoNintendo coverage)
label: snippet
claim: Sakurai's YouTube channel has a video on hit stop in Smash Ultimate; only news coverage seen, contents not verified.

title: Illustrative Rendering in Team Fortress 2 (Mitchell, Francke, Eng; NPAR 2007)
label: developer
claim: Valve on its own game. Shading designed 'to quickly convey geometric information... using variation in luminance and hue, so that game players are consistently able to visually read the scene and identify other players in a variety of lighting conditions'. Nine classes' silhouettes 'carefully designed to be very distinct'; validated in concept phase by checking characters are identifiable as pure silhouettes with no internal shading. Silhouettes emphasized with rim highlights rather than dark outlines; shadows go cool not black; high-frequency detail omitted; clothing folds echo silhouette shapes. Teams: red = warm colours, natural materials, angular geometry; blue = cool colours, industrial materials, orthogonal forms. Colours 'border on realism, but with increased saturation and value contrast'; muted colours dominate with small saturated areas. Claims photoreal high-frequency detail can overpower designers' ability to emphasise gameplay features via value. No player data in the paper; a design rationale.

title: Aesthetic-usability effect (search summary of Kurosu & Kashimura 1995, Tractinsky 1997/2000)
label: snippet
claim: Kurosu & Kashimura: 26 ATM layouts rated by 252 subjects, apparent usability correlated with beauty r=.589 (ratings only, no use). Tractinsky 1997 replicated in Israel, r~0.59. Tractinsky, Katz, Ikar 2000: aesthetics affected post-use perceived usability, actual usability did not. Seen via search summary.

title: Changing only the aesthetic features of a product can affect its apparent usability (Monk & Lelos 2007)
label: research
claim: Three experiments with painted can openers (students and older people): products rated more beautiful were rated more usable; in Exp 1 and 3, a purely cosmetic change (paint) significantly raised usability ratings, answering the correlation-vs-cause criticism. Also notes Tractinsky 2000 manipulated usability (9 s delay, keys needing a second click) and those versions were rated less beautiful, i.e. 'usable is beautiful', which says nothing about the reverse. Product is a physical can opener, not software or games. Read abstract and intro via PDF text.

title: Brewster, Chohan, Brown: Tactile feedback for mobile interactions (CHI 2007)
label: snippet
claim: Search summary: tactile feedback on PDA touchscreen keyboard gave significantly more text entered, fewer errors, more errors corrected than no tactile; on a moving underground train only errors corrected improved significantly, though users subjectively liked it. Hoggan, Brewster, Johnston CHI 2008: tactile on touchscreen brought finger text entry close to a physical keyboard. A later York study found no significant effect of feedback mode on speed/accuracy and nearly half preferred no aural or haptic feedback. n and statistics not seen.

title: Xbox Accessibility Guideline 103: additional channels for visual and audio cues
label: guideline
claim: 'Color alone should never be used to represent information'; pair colour with shape, pattern, icon or text; if colour is primary (rarity tiers), let players choose colours; greying out an unavailable control needs a second signal (lock icon, 'Not available' text); critical visual content needs at least one non-visual channel and vice versa; haptics only in addition to another cue because players disable or lack them; simulators (Color Oracle) are internal aids, not a substitute for testing with colourblind players; cataracts are more common than colourblindness.

title: Xbox Accessibility Guideline 102: contrast
label: guideline
claim: Minimum contrast: 4.5:1 for standard text/visual elements; 3:1 for large text (console 1080p from 52 px, PC/VR 1080p from 36 px); inactive-element text still 3:1; high-contrast mode 7:1 for all UI; measure against the lowest-contrast part of a non-solid background.

title: Game Accessibility Guidelines: no essential information by fixed colour alone
label: guideline
claim: Rated Basic (vision). Convey colour-coded info with text, symbol, pattern or shape too; where not enough, let players customise colours; test with a colour-blindness simulator.

title: Celeste & Forgiveness (coyote time / jump buffering, search summary)
label: snippet
claim: Search summary: Maddy Thorson's 2020 thread describes coyote time (jump allowed briefly after leaving a ledge) and jump buffering. Frame counts reported by third-party sites disagree (5 vs 6 frames coyote); community defaults ~5 frames coyote, ~7 buffer at 60 fps. Not confirmed by the developer.

title: Apple HIG: Playing haptics
label: guideline
claim: Use haptic patterns by their documented meaning; use haptics consistently so each ties causally to an action (same pattern for failure and for level-complete confuses); complement other feedback, matching haptic intensity and sharpness to the animation; avoid overuse ('occasionally just right, tiresome when frequent'); 'often the best haptic experience is one that people may not be conscious of, but miss when it's turned off'; short haptics for discrete events, long ones dilute meaning; make haptics optional and the app enjoyable without them. Transient vs continuous events, tunable sharpness and intensity. No measured data.

title: Game Anim (Jonathan Cooper) page on anticipation and recoil
label: practitioner
claim: Page text: player-character anticipation 'tend to be fast for the PC so as to not delay too long after the joypad input'; NPC anticipation longer so players can react; 'the feel of the PC should always take precedence over the aesthetics of the animations'; too slow a reaction makes the PC 'sluggish and unresponsive'; recoil returns to a pose for smooth transition. No frame counts. Attribution to Cooper comes from the site and search summary, the fetched text did not name him.

title: The Art of Game Polish: Developers Speak (Game Developer, 2009)
label: developer
claim: BioWare, Epic, Obsidian, Robomodo staff on polish. Darrah: 'what defines polish in a game is a consistency of experience'. Kowalkowski: adding things players never notice but notice when missing. Rubalcalba: 'Polish is no small task; it is just about small unseen things.' Fergusson: polish is the final stretch and needs dedicated schedule time, not leftover buffer; define a quality bar because polishing can continue forever; triage late fixes because each can introduce bugs. Dwyer: list what needs polish, estimate each, rank by effect on gameplay. 2009, AAA console era; interview summary, no measurement.

title: Indie Polish: Making the Most of the Last 10% (Mike Bithell, GDC 2015)
label: developer
claim: Talk description only: indies spend long on the core and may not spend enough finishing it; talk covers polish on Thomas Was Alone and Volume. Content is members-only; nothing on cost in the description.

title: Jota, Ng, Dietz & Wigdor, How fast is fast enough? Latency in direct-touch pointing tasks (CHI 2013), full PDF read
label: research
claim: Two studies on a high-speed touch prototype with artificial latency. Experiment 1 (performance): 45 participants (28 male, age 19-52), within-subject dragging of a 2 cm cursor box to a target, latency 1, 10, 25, 50 ms x width 3/4/5 cm x distance 3.5/8.5/15 cm x 8 reps = 12,960 trials. Latency main effect on throughput F(3,132)=114.65 and movement time F(3,132)=45.13, both p<.001; errors also rose (F(3,132)=25.67 p<.001); worse for smaller and farther targets (latency x width F(6,264)=2.58 p=.019; latency x distance F(6,264)=3.48 p=.02). Throughput: 1 vs 10 ms not different (p=1.0) but every other pair p<.001 (1 vs 50: 0.109 bit/s difference); mean movement time at 1 ms 751.3 ms against 747.6 ms predicted by the 10/25/50 ms line (R2=.956), so the authors conclude there may be no performance floor for dragging. Most of the cost falls in the final refinement phase (time inside the target). Experiment 2 (perception of the tap/land-on feedback, not of dragging): 20 of the same participants, adaptive-staircase JND against a 1 ms reference at 75% correct; JND ranged 20-100 ms, mean 64 ms (SD 24). No participant could tell latency below 20 ms from 1 ms and 85% could not tell 40 ms from 1 ms. Tap-only input at 50 ms vs 1 ms costs only about 7% response time. Authors' summary: ~20 ms touch-to-display is enough that most users do not perceive it when input is tapping; dragging may need as little as 2.38 ms (their citation of Ng et al.'s perception figure, not measured here); events older than 10 ms mid-drag reduce performance. The '25 ms' and '24 ms' figures in circulation come from Deber 2015's paraphrase, not from Jota's text. Limits: pointing on a prototype with no other latency source, one-finger Fitts-style tasks, 20 participants in the perception test, JND is relative to a 1 ms reference rather than an absolute floor.

title: Deber, Jota, Forlines & Wigdor, How Much Faster is Fast Enough? (CHI 2015), full PDF read
label: research
claim: Two JND-style experiments on a high-speed touch rig (as low as 0.29 ms latency; indirect form factor made by mirror to a wall screen). Experiment 1: 24 sessions (12 drag, 12 tap) by 14 right-handed university participants (6 male, mean age 28), form factor between sessions, staircase JND at 75% correct. Mean latency JND: direct drag 11 ms, indirect drag 55 ms, direct tap 69 ms, indirect tap 96 ms. Main effect of task F(1,22)=55.79 p<.001 (drag 33 ms vs tap 82 ms) and of form factor F(1,22)=48.43 p<.001 (direct 40 ms vs indirect 75 ms); no interaction. Within drag, direct vs indirect F(1,11)=77.11 p<.001; within tap F(1,11)=9.44 p=.011. Authors say their values bracket the literature: Ng et al. 6.04 ms (direct drag), Jota 2013 64 ms (direct tap), textbook 100 ms (indirect tap) all fall inside their 95% confidence intervals, so the 2-100 ms disagreement is task and form factor, not error. Experiment 2: 15 participants (7 male, mean age 25), 24 sessions, which of two latencies is lower, base latency 8.3-166.7 ms (multiples of a 60 Hz frame) and improvements of 8.3-83.3 ms. Dragging: direct 86.9% correct vs indirect 76.3% (F(1,11)=47.56 p<.001), 8.3 ms improvements noticeable from a wide range of baselines in direct drag; any 16.7 ms (one frame) improvement easily seen in direct drag. Tapping: about 68% correct overall (69.3% direct, 67.1% indirect, form factor n.s.); at base latency <=33.3 ms little perceivable improvement; above that, improvements of 2+ frames (33 ms) are noticed and 0.5-1 frame mostly not. Perception only; the authors list performance benefit of the improvements as next work. Limits: small university samples (12 sessions per cell), 2 cm square white feedback on a lab rig, no measure of whether noticing matters for play. Figures like '69 ms tap / 11 ms drag' are direct-touch JNDs from this paper (direct only; indirect 96/55).
